{{Short description|Concept in statistics}}
In [[probability]] and [[statistics]], a '''compound probability distribution''' (also known as a '''[[mixture distribution]]''' or '''contagious distribution''') is the [[probability distribution]] that results from assuming that a [[random variable]] is distributed according to some parametrized distribution, with (some of) the parameters of that distribution themselves being random variables.
If the parameter is a [[scale parameter]], the resulting mixture is also called a '''scale mixture'''.

The compound distribution ("unconditional distribution") is the result of [[marginal distribution|marginalizing]] (integrating) over the ''latent'' random variable(s) representing the parameter(s) of the parametrized distribution ("conditional distribution").

==Definition==

A '''compound probability distribution''' is the probability distribution that results from assuming that a random variable <math>X</math> is distributed according to some parametrized distribution <math>F</math> with an unknown parameter <math>\theta</math> that is again distributed according to some other distribution <math>G</math>. The resulting distribution <math>H</math> is said to be the distribution that results from compounding <math>F</math> with <math>G</math>. The parameter's distribution <math>G</math> is also called the '''mixing distribution''' or '''latent distribution'''. Technically, the ''unconditional'' distribution <math>H</math> results from ''[[marginal distribution|marginalizing]]'' over <math>G</math>, i.e., from integrating out the unknown parameter(s) <math>\theta</math>. Its [[probability density function]] is given by:

:<math>p_H(x) = {\displaystyle \int\limits p_F(x|\theta)\,p_G(\theta) \operatorname{d}\!\theta}</math>

The same formula applies analogously if some or all of the variables are vectors.

From the above formula, one can see that a compound distribution essentially is a special case of a [[marginal distribution]]: The ''[[joint probability distribution|joint distribution]]'' of <math>x</math> and <math>\theta</math> is given by 
<math>p(x,\theta)=p(x|\theta)p(\theta)</math>, and the compound results as its marginal distribution:
<math> {\textstyle p(x) = \int p(x,\theta) \operatorname{d}\!\theta } </math>.
If the domain of <math>\theta</math> is discrete, then the distribution is again a special case of a [[mixture distribution]].

==Properties==
===General===
The compound distribution <math>H</math> will depend on the specific expression of each distribution, as well as which parameter of <math>F</math> is distributed according to the distribution <math>G</math>, and the parameters of <math>H</math> will include any parameters of <math>G</math> that are not marginalized, or integrated, out.
The [[support (mathematics)|support]] of <math>H</math> is the same as that of <math>F</math>, and if the latter is a two-parameter distribution parameterized with the mean and variance, some general properties exist.

===Mean and variance===
The compound distribution's first two [[moment (mathematics)|moments]] are given by the [[law of total expectation]] and the [[law of total variance]]:

<math display="block"> \operatorname{E}_H[X] = \operatorname{E}_G\bigl[\operatorname{E}_F[X|\theta]\bigr] </math>

<math display="block"> \operatorname{Var}_H(X) = \operatorname{E}_G\bigl[\operatorname{Var}_F(X|\theta)\bigr] + \operatorname{Var}_G\bigl(\operatorname{E}_F[X|\theta]\bigr) </math> 

If the mean of <math>F</math> is distributed as <math>G</math>, which in turn has mean <math>\mu</math> and variance <math>\sigma^2</math> the expressions above imply <math> \operatorname{E}_H[X] = \operatorname{E}_G[\theta] = \mu </math> and <math> \operatorname{Var}_H(X) = \operatorname{Var}_F(X|\theta) + \operatorname{Var}_G(Y) = \tau^2 + \sigma^2</math>, where <math>\tau^2</math> is the variance of <math>F</math>.

===Proof===
let <math>F</math> and <math>G</math> be probability distributions parameterized with mean and variance as<math display="block">\begin{align}
x &\sim \mathcal{F}(\theta,\tau^2) \\
\theta &\sim \mathcal{G}(\mu,\sigma^2)
\end{align} </math>then denoting the probability density functions as <math> f(x|\theta) = p_F(x|\theta)</math> and <math>g(\theta) = p_G(\theta)</math> respectively, and <math>h(x)</math> being the probability density of <math>H</math> we have<math display="block">\begin{align}
\operatorname{E}_H[X] = \int_F x h(x)dx &= \int_F x  \int_G f(x|\theta) g(\theta) d\theta dx \\
                                        &= \int_G \int_F x f(x|\theta) dx\ g(\theta)  d\theta \\
                                        &= \int_G \operatorname{E}_F[X|\theta] g(\theta)  d\theta
\end{align} </math>and we have from the parameterization <math>\mathcal{F}</math> and <math>\mathcal{G}</math> that<math display="block">\begin{align}
\operatorname{E}_F[X|\theta] &= \int_F x f(x|\theta)dx = \theta \\
\operatorname{E}_G[\theta] &= \int_G \theta g(\theta)d\theta = \mu
\end{align} </math>and therefore the mean of the compound distribution <math> \operatorname{E}_H[X] = \mu </math> as per the expression for its first moment above.


The variance of <math>H</math> is given by <math>\operatorname{E}_H[X^2] - (\operatorname{E}_H[X])^2</math>, and<math display="block">\begin{align}
\operatorname{E}_H[X^2] = \int_F x^2 h(x)dx &= \int_F x^2  \int_G f(x|\theta) g(\theta) d\theta dx \\
                                        &= \int_G g(\theta)\int_F x^2 f(x|\theta) dx\   d\theta \\
                                        &= \int_G g(\theta)(\tau^2+\theta^2)d\theta\\
                                        &= \tau^2\int_G g(\theta)d\theta+\int_Gg(\theta)\theta^2d\theta\\
                                        &= \tau^2+(\sigma^2+\mu^2),
\end{align} </math>given the fact that <math>\int_F x^2 f(x\mid \theta) dx=\operatorname{E}_F[X^2\mid \theta]=\operatorname{Var}_F(X\mid\theta)+(\operatorname{E}_F[X\mid \theta])^2 </math> and <math>\int_G \theta^2 g(\theta)d\theta=\operatorname{E}_G[\theta^2 ]=\operatorname{Var}_G(\theta) + (\operatorname{E}_G[\theta])^2 </math>. Finally we get<math display="block">\begin{align}
\operatorname{Var}_H(X) &= \operatorname{E}_H[X^2] - (\operatorname{E}_H[X])^2 \\
                        &= \tau^2 + \sigma^2
\end{align} </math>

==Applications==
===Testing===
Distributions of common [[test statistic]]s result as compound distributions under their null hypothesis, for example in [[Student's t-test]] (where the test statistic results as the ratio of a [[normal distribution|normal]] and a [[chi-squared distribution|chi-squared]] random variable), or in the [[F-test]] (where the test statistic is the ratio of two [[chi-squared distribution|chi-squared]] random variables).

===Overdispersion modeling===
Compound distributions are useful for modeling outcomes exhibiting [[overdispersion]], i.e., a greater amount of variability than would be expected under a certain model. For example, count data are commonly modeled using the [[Poisson distribution]], whose variance is equal to its mean. The distribution may be generalized by allowing for variability in its [[rate parameter]], implemented via a [[gamma distribution]], which results in a marginal [[negative binomial distribution]]. This distribution is similar in its shape to the Poisson distribution, but it allows for larger variances. Similarly, a [[binomial distribution]] may be generalized to allow for additional variability by compounding it with a [[beta distribution]] for its success probability parameter, which results in a [[beta-binomial distribution]].

===Bayesian inference===
Besides ubiquitous marginal distributions that may be seen as special cases of compound distributions, 
in [[Bayesian inference]], compound distributions arise when, in the notation above, ''F'' represents the distribution of future observations and ''G'' is the [[posterior distribution]] of the parameters of ''F'', given the information in a set of observed data. This gives a [[posterior predictive distribution]]. Correspondingly, for the [[prior predictive distribution]], ''F'' is the distribution of a new data point while ''G'' is the [[prior distribution]] of the parameters.

===Convolution===
[[Convolution]] of probability distributions (to derive the probability distribution of sums of random variables) may also be seen as a special case of compounding; here the sum's distribution essentially results from considering one summand as a random [[location parameter]] for the other summand.<ref name="RoeverFriede2017">{{cite journal|last1=Röver|first1=C.|last2=Friede|first2=T.|title= Discrete approximation of a mixture distribution via restricted divergence|journal=Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics|volume=26|issue=1|year=2017|pages=217–222|doi=10.1080/10618600.2016.1276840|doi-access=free|arxiv=1602.04060}}</ref>

==Computation==
Compound distributions derived from [[exponential family]] distributions often have a closed form.
If analytical integration is not possible, numerical methods may be necessary.

Compound distributions may relatively easily be investigated using [[Monte Carlo method]]s, i.e., by generating random samples. It is often easy to generate random numbers from the 
distributions <math>p(\theta)</math> as well as <math>p(x|\theta)</math> and then utilize these to perform ''[[collapsed Gibbs sampling]]'' to generate samples from <math>p(x)</math>.

A compound distribution may usually also be approximated to a sufficient degree by a [[mixture distribution]] using a finite number of mixture components, allowing to derive approximate density, distribution function etc.<ref name="RoeverFriede2017" />

[[estimation theory|Parameter estimation]] ([[Maximum-likelihood estimation|maximum-likelihood]] or [[Maximum a posteriori estimation|maximum-a-posteriori]] estimation) within a compound distribution model may sometimes be simplified by utilizing the [[EM-algorithm]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Gelman|first1=A.|last2=Carlin|first2=J. B.|last3=Stern|first3=H.|last4=Rubin|first4=D. B.|title=Bayesian Data Analysis|edition=1st|publisher=Chapman & Hall / CRC|place=Boca Raton|year=1997|chapter=9.5 ''Finding marginal posterior modes using EM and related algorithms''|page=276}}</ref>

==Examples==
* '''Gaussian scale mixtures''':<ref name="LeeMcLachlan2019">{{cite book|last1=Lee|first1=S.X.|last2=McLachlan|first2=G.J. |title=Wiley StatsRef: Statistics Reference Online |chapter=Scale Mixture Distribution |year=2019|pages=1–16 |doi=10.1002/9781118445112.stat08201|isbn=978-1-118-44511-2 }}</ref><ref name="Gneiting1997">{{cite journal|last1=Gneiting|first1=T.|title=Normal scale mixtures and dual probability densities|journal=Journal of Statistical Computation and Simulation|volume=59|issue=4|year=1997|pages=375–384|doi=10.1080/00949659708811867}}</ref>
** Compounding a [[normal distribution]] with [[variance]] distributed according to an [[inverse gamma distribution]] (or equivalently, with [[precision (statistics)|precision]] distributed as a [[gamma distribution]]) yields a non-standardized '''[[Student's t-distribution]]'''.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Mood|first1=A. M.|last2=Graybill|first2=F. A.|last3=Boes|first3=D. C.|title=Introduction to the theory of statistics|edition=3rd|publisher=McGraw-Hill|place=New York|year=1974}}</ref>  This distribution has the same symmetrical shape as a normal distribution with the same central point, but has greater variance and [[heavy tail]]s.
** Compounding a [[Gaussian distribution|Gaussian (or normal) distribution]] with variance distributed according to an [[exponential distribution]] (or with standard deviation according to a [[Rayleigh distribution]]) yields a '''[[Laplace distribution]]'''.  More generally, compounding a Gaussian (or normal) distribution with variance distributed according to a [[gamma distribution]] yields a '''[[variance-gamma distribution]]'''.
** Compounding a [[Gaussian distribution]] with variance distributed according to an [[exponential distribution]] whose rate parameter is itself distributed according to a [[gamma distribution]] yields a '''[[Normal-exponential-gamma distribution]]'''. (This involves two compounding stages. The variance itself then follows a [[Lomax distribution]]; see below.)
** Compounding a [[Gaussian distribution]] with standard deviation distributed according to a [[Inverse distribution#Inverse uniform distribution|(standard) inverse uniform distribution]] yields a '''[[Slash distribution]]'''.
** Compounding a [[Gaussian distribution|Gaussian (normal) distribution]] with a [[Kolmogorov–Smirnov_test#Kolmogorov_distribution | Kolmogorov distribution]] yields a '''[[logistic distribution]]'''.<ref>{{Citation | last1=Andrews | first1=D.F. | last2=Mallows | first2=C.L. | year=1974 | title=Scale mixtures of normal distributions | journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B | volume=36 | issue=1 | pages=99–102 | doi=10.1111/j.2517-6161.1974.tb00989.x}}</ref><ref name="LeeMcLachlan2019" />
* '''other Gaussian mixtures''':
** Compounding a [[Gaussian distribution]] with [[mean]] distributed according to another [[Gaussian distribution]] yields (again) a '''[[Gaussian distribution]]'''.
** Compounding a [[Gaussian distribution]] with [[mean]] distributed according to a shifted [[exponential distribution]] yields an '''[[exponentially modified Gaussian distribution]]'''.

* Compounding a [[Bernoulli distribution]] with probability of success <math>p</math> distributed according to a distribution <math>X</math> that has a defined expected value yields a Bernoulli distribution with success probability <math>E[X]</math>. An interesting consequence is that the dispersion of <math>X</math> does not influence the dispersion of the resulting compound distribution.  
* Compounding a [[binomial distribution]] with probability of success distributed according to a [[beta distribution]] yields a '''[[beta-binomial distribution]]'''.  It possesses three parameters, a parameter <math>n</math> (number of samples) from the binomial distribution and [[shape parameter]]s <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math> from the beta distribution.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Johnson|first1=N. L.|last2=Kemp|first2=A. W.|author2-link=Adrienne W. Kemp|last3=Kotz|first3=S.|title=Univariate discrete distributions|edition=3rd|publisher=Wiley|place=New York|year=2005|chapter=6.2.2|page=253}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Gelman|first1=A.|last2=Carlin|first2=J. B.|last3=Stern|first3=H.|last4=Dunson|first4=D. B.|last5=Vehtari|first5=A.|last6=Rubin|first6=D. B.|title=Bayesian Data Analysis|edition=3rd|publisher=Chapman & Hall / CRC|place=Boca Raton|year=2014|bibcode=2014bda..book.....G }}</ref>
* Compounding a [[multinomial distribution]] with probability vector distributed according to a [[Dirichlet distribution]] yields a '''[[Dirichlet-multinomial distribution]]'''.
* Compounding a [[Poisson distribution]] with [[rate parameter]] distributed according to a [[gamma distribution]] yields a '''[[negative binomial distribution]]'''.<ref>{{cite journal|year=1987|title=Negative binomial and mixed Poisson regression|journal=The Canadian Journal of Statistics|volume=15|issue=3|pages=209–225|last1=Lawless|first1=J.F.|doi=10.2307/3314912|jstor=3314912}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Teich, M. C.|author2=Diament, P.|title=Multiply stochastic representations for K distributions and their Poisson transforms|journal=Journal of the Optical Society of America A|date=1989|volume=6|issue=1|pages=80–91|doi=10.1364/JOSAA.6.000080|bibcode=1989JOSAA...6...80T}}</ref>
* Compounding a [[Poisson distribution]] with rate parameter distributed according to an [[exponential distribution]] yields a '''[[geometric distribution]]'''.
* Compounding an [[exponential distribution]] with its [[rate parameter]] distributed according to a [[gamma distribution]] yields a '''[[Lomax distribution]]'''.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Johnson|first1=N. L.|last2=Kotz|first2=S.|last3=Balakrishnan|first3=N.|title=Continuous univariate distributions|edition=2nd|volume=1|publisher=Wiley|place=New York|year=1994|chapter=20 ''Pareto distributions''|page=573}}</ref>
* Compounding a [[gamma distribution]] with [[rate parameter|inverse scale parameter]] distributed according to another [[gamma distribution]] yields a three-parameter '''[[Beta prime distribution#Compound gamma distribution|beta prime distribution]]'''.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Dubey | first1 = S. D. | doi = 10.1007/BF02613934 | title = Compound gamma, beta and F distributions | journal = Metrika | volume = 16 | pages = 27–31 | year = 1970 }}</ref>
* Compounding a [[half-normal distribution]] with its [[scale parameter]] distributed according to a [[Rayleigh distribution]] yields an '''[[exponential distribution]]'''. This follows immediately from the [[Laplace distribution]] resulting as a [[normal distribution|normal]] scale mixture; see above. The roles of conditional and mixing distributions may also be exchanged here; consequently, compounding a [[Rayleigh distribution]] with its scale parameter distributed according to a [[half-normal distribution]] ''also'' yields an [[exponential distribution]].
* A [[gamma distribution|Gamma(k=2,θ) - distributed]] random variable whose [[scale parameter]] θ again is [[uniform distribution (continuous)|uniformly]] distributed marginally yields an '''[[exponential distribution]]'''.

==Similar terms==

The notion of "compound distribution" as used e.g. in the definition of a [[Compound Poisson distribution]] or [[Compound Poisson process]] is different from the definition found in this article. The meaning in this article corresponds to what is used in e.g. [[Bayesian hierarchical modeling]].

The special case for compound probability distributions where the parametrized distribution <math>F</math> is the [[Poisson distribution]] is also called [[mixed Poisson distribution]].
